---
title: "convinterp"
subtitle: "The Python port, with a Rust core"
jupyter: python3
---

convinterp brings the convolution kernels to Python. The interface works with NumPy arrays; the
numerics run in a compiled Rust core, with the same exact polynomial kernels as the Julia
package. Every released feature is tested against ConvolutionInterpolations.jl, the reference
implementation, so the two give the same results to the last bit of the boundary coefficients.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import importlib.metadata
print(f"This site was rendered against version {importlib.metadata.version('convinterp')}.")
```

## Installation

```bash
pip install convinterp
```

Prebuilt wheels are available for Linux, macOS and Windows, on x86_64 and ARM, so no Rust
toolchain is needed. NumPy is the only dependency.

## What the port has

The port is an alpha release, growing feature by feature towards the Julia package. The
[feature matrix](../features.qmd) is the authoritative list; in short, what is there is
interpolation on uniform grids in any number of dimensions, with every derivative and integral
order the kernels support, mixed per axis, and the automatic boundary detection. Nonuniform
grids, smoothing, resampling and scattered data are on the roadmap, in that order.

Everything is reached through one function, `convolution_interpolation`, which returns an
interpolant that is called like a function:

| Call | What it does | Concept page |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `convolution_interpolation(x, y)` | Interpolates 1D data on a uniform grid | [Interpolation](../concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| `convolution_interpolation((x, y), data)` | Interpolates gridded data in any number of dimensions | [Interpolation](../concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| `convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=k)` | A derivative of the interpolant, evaluated analytically | [Derivatives](../concepts/derivatives.qmd) |
| `convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-k)` | An integral of the interpolant, anchored at the first knot | [Integrals](../concepts/integrals.qmd) |
| `convolution_interpolation(x, y, bc="poly")` | Chooses the boundary extrapolation, per side or per axis | [Boundaries](../concepts/boundaries.qmd) |

The `kernel` argument selects the kernel, `"a0"` to `"a7"` and `"b5"` to `"b13"`; the
[interpolation page](../concepts/interpolation.qmd) has the table of their degrees, continuity
and convergence orders, and the [API reference](api.qmd) has every argument.

## What is specific to Python

- **NumPy broadcasting.** An interpolant accepts a number or an array of any shape and returns
  the same shape; in more dimensions the coordinate arrays broadcast against each other like
  NumPy arrays, so a column of x values against a row of y values evaluates a whole table.
- **Float64 only.** The Rust core works in double precision; the generic element types of the
  Julia package are not ported.
- **Errors are `ValueError`s.** Nonuniform knots, points outside the data range, and derivative
  orders a kernel does not support all raise a `ValueError` that says what is wrong.
- **No extrapolation yet.** Points must lie inside the data range; the `extrap` keyword of the
  Julia package has no counterpart yet.
- **Plotting.** The examples on this site use Matplotlib; an interpolant evaluated on
  `np.linspace` arrays plots like any NumPy function.
